- During September official 3-month prices traded within in a relatively narrow range, fluctuating from the month’s high of $6448/t on the 8<sup>th</sup> to the month’s low of $5901/t on the 28<sup>th</sup> .  However, this moderate $548/t overall monthly trading range masks the fact that day to day volatility has remained a feature of the market with min/max variations in official 3-month quotes ranging from -$239/t to + $219/t as of the 29<sup>th</sup> . 

- Uncertainty remains a key feature of the copper market and, to our mind, the biggest worry aside from there being no meaningful pick up in consumption within the mature economies relates to the massive disconnect between Chinese apparent consumption (+48%) and the country’s estimated refined consumption (+22%) year on year thus far through August.  This differential is equivalent to ~850kt Cu and the major unknown is who actually holds these stocks and, therefore, what the catalyst(s) would be for releasing this copper? 

- We forecast that global refined copper consumption will decline by 2.8% this year to ~17.4Mt.  Next year however, demand is expected to recover by 3.9% to 18Mt, while in 2011 stronger growth is projected with global demand increasing by 6.2% to just over 19.1Mt.  The recovery will reflect the combination of pent up consumer and business demand, re-stocking, and the coming to fruition of many government-backed infrastructure initiatives. 

- Spot concentrate activity during September was a little quiet with only four tenders of note, these being from mines in Bulgaria, Laos, Peru and South Africa.  On the basis of two tender results spot selling terms between miners and traders have been seen in the range $17-19/t & 1.7-1.9c/lb.

## Market Developments 

**Increase in volatility during September** During September official 3-month prices traded within in a relatively narrow range, fluctuating from the month’s high of $6448/t on the 8<sup>th</sup> to the month’s low of $5901/t on the 28<sup>th</sup> .  However, this moderate $548/t overall monthly trading range masks the fact that day to day volatility has remained a feature of

the market with min/max variations in official 3-month quotes ranging from -$239/t to + $219/t as of the 29<sup>th</sup> .  Similar to last month, these variable trading conditions were fuelled by mixed sentiment on account of uncertainty amongst market participants.  Prices rallied on three separate occasions during the month, largely reflecting the release of positive macro economic data and renewed concerns over potential supply disruptions.  However, while the release of positive economic data was price supportive, the release of negative data was also responsible for pushing quotes lower.  Indeed the news of negative US housing data in recent days as well as talk of massive Chinese metal stockpiles were partly responsible for prompting a major sell-off in copper which resulted in official 3-month quotes falling from $6310/t on the 22<sup>nd</sup> to around $6100/t t at the time of writing. 

**Prices supported by positive macro economic data** The first price rally of the month occurred between the 3<sup>rd</sup> and the 8<sup>th</sup> when official 3-month quotes rose by a net $364/t, up from $6084/t to $6313/t.  The main impetus for the surge was the news that Chinese passenger car sales jumped by 90%, year on year in August while year-to-date (Jan-Aug) sales were up by 29% from a year earlier.  Other contributing factors to the rally included a depreciating US dollar and news of a mudslide at Anglo American’s Los Bronces copper mine in Chile.  As it transpired, it was a road leading to the mine that was affected and not production.  The second rally saw prices (3m) rising by $211/t over the course of three days, from $6140/t on the 14<sup>th</sup> to $6302/t on the 17<sup>th</sup> .  Positive macro economic data from China was a contributing factor with data relating to construction activity.  It was reported that Chinese floor space under construction rose by 39.5% in August from a year earlier, following an 8% annual rise in July.  This was the first time since 1997 that floor space under construction had increased on an annual basis during these two months.  Traditionally Chinese construction activity slows during the summer months because of less favourable weather conditions.  Prices were also boosted by the news that Japanese industrial production increased by 2.1% in July from a month earlier while the capacity utilisation rate, at 77.2% in July, rose for the fifth consecutive month. 

**The potential for additional supply disruptions increases** The third rally resulted in 3-month official quotes rising by $219/t on the 22<sup>nd</sup> to $6310/t.  In contrast to the previous two rallies this price rise was prompted by potential supply disruptions.  In Indonesia it was reported that there had been a pit wall failure at the Batu Hijau copper mine.  The pit remains closed while geotechnical studies are carried out, although milling operations continue with low grade stockpiled ore (see Production).  Meanwhile in Chile, prices were

supported by the news that workers at BHP Billiton’s Spence copper mine were waiting for a new labour offer from management following their request of a 5.5% pay increase and cash bonuses of ~$27k per person. At the time negotiations were expected to be difficult because of copper’s recent price strength. Subsequently, management has returned with a revised offer which was rejected by the workers. As a consequence the workers have threatened strike action next month. Elsewhere, workers at Antamina continue to operate the mine without a new contract (see Production). **Market sentiment dampened by poor US housing statistics** Official quotes during the month have been just as responsive to negative macro economic news as positive. **Flatter forward curve for copper** Copper’s forward curve has become flatter over the month, with prices not moving into backwardation until December next year i.e. fifteen months forward. This is in contrast to last month where forward spreads

switched into backwardation in March next year, i.e. just seven months forward.  The flatter curve suggests that the expectations of a tighter market during this period have subsided since the end of last month.  Therefore, while uncertainty continues to be a feature of the market, the latest forward spread data points to there being the perception of more risk to prices on the downside than on the upside. 

**Total exchange stock rise above 50kt for the second consecutive month** Total exchange stocks increased for the third consecutive month in September, rising by a net 58.2kt to 493kt as of the 29<sup>th</sup> .  The majority of the gain reflected a net uplift (45.7kt) in LME inventories to 345.7kt with a large portion of this tonnage (24.4kt) having been delivered into South Korean warehouses.  Indeed the net 23.6kt of material delivered into Busan during the month represented a record monthly increase within this location.  The large build up of tonnage is believed to be material that was originally destined for China which, due to the high level of Chinese imports received in recent months and a less favourable arbitrage, is not required presently.  Market sources also suggested that the build up in Asia was part of a premia play ahead of the annual premia negotiations due to start in London next month.  Producers will obviously be keen to keep tonnages in European warehouses at a minimum in order to support the case for higher annual European premia in 2010.  Not that this is likely to happen if, indeed, market rumours are accurate that Codelco has already concluded some 2010 European contracts at $80/t, i.e. the same level as this year.  Elsewhere in Europe and the US, LME inventories rose by a net 6.9kt, to 68.4kt, and 11.9kt to 224.6kt respectively. 

**Chinese inventories reach their highest level since March 2004** On Comex, inventories rose by a net 0.4kt, to 48.7kt, while in China SHFE stocks increased by a net 12.1kt to 98.7kt, their highest level since March 2004.  The upsurge in SHFE inventories is not surprising in light of the record imports of refined metal seen recently.  This build-up in Chinese stocks is more a reflection of the over-importing of refined copper, partly as a result of favourable arbitrage trading conditions and tightening scrap availability, than any significant decline in underlying demand. 

**Expected pick-up in European spot activity has not happened** The European physical market remained extremely quiet during September despite expectations of a pick-up in demand following the summer shutdown period.  There were some reports of business taking place in Italy but this was for a small amount only and at a premium of $80/t, down from

**Uncertainty key feature** As noted earlier uncertainty remains a key feature of the copper market and, to our mind, the biggest worry aside from there being no meaningful pick up in consumption within the mature economies relates to the massive disconnect between Chinese apparent consumption (+48%) and the country’s estimated refined consumption (+22%) year on year thus far through August. This differential is equivalent to ~850kt Cu and the major unknown is who actually holds these stocks and, therefore, what the catalyst(s) would be for releasing this copper? Estimates of SRB intake this year vary from 150kt to 250kt, although according to our enquiries the figure is probably closer to the lower end of this range. Commercial stocks, including re-stocking, are likely to have increased by 100kt -150kt while exchange stocks were up by almost 70kt. There is little evidence of a massive build in copper stocks by the various regional governments (whose main objective has been to support ailing producers of other metals that are overtly in substantial oversupply this year). This leaves a significant tonnage (400kt to 550kt in round numbers) that appears to be in the hands of traders and (other?) speculators whose purchase prices and profit objectives will no doubt vary considerably from holder to holder. At one extreme if these speculators believe that there is little further scope for higher prices and they sell en masse then this would no doubt have a very negative impa

ct on prices. At the other extreme, if the general view is that copper’s longer term fundamentals are sufficiently positive and the financing of these stocks is not problematic then the short/medium term outlook for copper prices should remain positive. However, perhaps the most likely outcome is that these speculators will sell a proportion of their metal holdings into upcoming price rallies which may dampen or perhaps cap the upside to these rallies. Whatever the outcome overall inventories are far higher than is indicated by exchange stocks and current prices are well above what is justified based on fundamentals alone. **Global surplus forecast for fourth consecutive year in 2010** For 2009 overall we forecast that prices will average $4930/t ($2.24c/lb), down from $6966/t ($3.16/lb) in 2008, while overall stocks will rise from 50 days of consumption in 2008 to 65 days. We expect that for the fourth consecutive year, the copper market will register an overall metal surplus in 2010. Whilst refined consumption is forecast to increase by 3.9%, even after our mine disruption allowance of 6%, supply should outstrip consumption resulting in a global market surplus of just over 500kt. On this basis stocks will rise to an equivalent of 73 days of consumption with prices projected to average $5300/t ($2.40/lb). Metals Market Service Monthly Update – September 2009 Page 6 of 26 Copper Monthly Update ## Economic Developments **US industrial outlook continues to improve** Leading indicators for the US economy have continued to improve over the past month, reinforcing our expectations that industry in the USA has started down the long road to recovery. Industrial production in August increased by 0.8% month on month, following on from the 1.0% increase in July, marking the first occasion since the end of 2007 where IP has expanded in consecutive months. However, it is worth remembering that output remains significantly down (-10.7%) from a year earlier. One of the primary drivers of increased output has been the automotive sector, where production of cars and commercial vehicles rocketed by 45% from July, although it remained 20% below the levels of August 2008. **Inventories provide the boost to output** The other primary reason that we have seen a return to expansion in industrial production is inventories. Heavy destocking has occurred right through the value chain in the past year, reaching a point where inventories have in some cases reached excessively low levels. With demand firming faster than many had expected, producers have been scrambling to increase output to close the gap with sales. We continue to expect the inventory cycle to be the key driver of short-term industrial output, pushing it further along the road to recovery through into early 2010. **The US consumer remains the key area for concern** An inventory boost to production can only be transitory in nature, typically lasting around 6-9 months. In order to transition into a more sustainable period of recovery, underlying consumption needs to significantly improve. There have been some encouraging signs of an improvement in consumption. US retail sales rose by a greater than expected 2.7% in August, and although they were still down by 5.3% YoY, this was an improvement over the average of -9.2% in 1H09. However, we would caution that this does not yet imply improved strength in underlying consumption. Much of the August retail sales increase can be attributed to vehicle sales thanks to the _Cash for Clunkers_ scheme. Sales actually declined in sectors such as building supplies and furniture, which are poor indications for the housing market. Employment, a key driver of consumption, continues to deteriorate. Unemployment rose to 9.7% in August, from 4.9% when the recession began in December 2007, and look s set to continue to rise through to mid-2010. Furthermore, US wage income in July was down by 5.1% from a year earlier; the fastest rate of contraction this year. The bottom line is that we do not expect US household consumption to improve significantly until well into next year, thereby tempering the gains in industrial output. **Autos drive Chinese industrial output higher** Industrial production growth in China accelerated in August to 12.3% YoY, up significantly from the 3.8% low seen at the start of the year. The star growth sector was once again automobiles. The government has halved the purchasing tax on passenger vehicles with engines smaller than 1.6 litres, and introduced a _Cash for Clunkers_ scheme, leading to a surge in demand for smaller vehicles in particular. In August, total vehicle production increased by a staggering 86% from a year earlier. It will be very difficult for China to maintain such growth rates in autos production, as demand will ease as the stimulus from the government’s policies wanes. **Indications of improving demand for Chinese export goods** It’s fair to say that China’s economic rebound in 2009 has been driven by significant government spending and large amounts of liquidity, counteracting the drop in export demand. As we have previously mentioned,

However, August industrial production figures for China did show some sign of recovery for industries heavily dependent upon exports. Output of electrical machinery increased by 13% year on year, and textile production also increased strongly. Metals Market Service Monthly Update – September 2009 Page 8 of 26 Copper Monthly Update ## Consumption **Economies continue to emerge from recession** A number of the world’s major economies appear to be emerging from recession. The global purchasing manager’s index for manufacturing cleared the 50 level in August and the services PMI is also improving. However, it remains extremely difficult to forecast the path of the recovery and its impact on copper demand. One school of thought is that because the contraction in global output was so rapid, the recovery will be equally rapid, and certainly the sharp rise in the manufacturing PMI, both globally and for a number of major economies, seems to lend credence to this theory. But the strength of the recovery owes much to the huge scale of fiscal stimulus packages that have been enacted by most of the world’s government’s, coupled with the very loose monetary policy that has helped pull the sting out of the recession. These stimulus packages have provided a foundation for growth and prompted manufacturers to begin to restock depleted inventories. However, this foundation is on unstable ground as, ultimately, decisions to re-stock or de-stock are not driven by inventory levels but sales. Without a recovery in sales there is a real danger that the current re-stocking inspired recovery in manufacturing could be followed by a further bout of de-stocking. The window for consumers to take over from the governments as the drivers of economic growth is quite small, and many of the world’s governments will, at some point in the 12-18 months, have to start raising taxes and cutting spending in order to begin the process of re-balancing national acco

**Recession has resulted in permanent cuts to copper demand in many countries** At a national level there will be considerable variation in the path of economic recovery, with the added complication that the severity of the recession will, in many countries, be the trigger for a permanent lowering of production capacity. In terms of copper, this means that in regions such as North America and Europe, the permanent closure of car plants will result in a permanent reduction in the demand for copper wiring and copper semi products. As a result, we are now forecasting that this year, US copper refined consumption will total ~1.7Mt, its lowest level since 1982, Western Europe is forecast to reach ~3Mt, its lowest level since 1988, whilst consumption in Japan is projected to fall to ~0.9Mt, its lowest level since 1975. **Healthy recovery in global copper demand forecast in 2010 and 2011** We forecast that global refined copper consumption will decline by 2.8% this year to ~17.4Mt. Next year however, demand is expected to recover by 3.9% to 18Mt, while in 2011 stronger growth is projected with global demand increasing by 6.2% to just over 19.1Mt. The recovery will reflect the combination of pent up consumer and business demand, re-stocking, and the coming to fruition of many government-backed infrastructure initiatives. The marked increase in 2011 will also reflect growing demand from the construction sector. While construction activity is expected to recover in 2010, the positive impact that this will have on copper demand will not be fully realised until the following year. This is because copper wire and cable and copper plumbing and heating tube are not installed in any new build until the latter stages of construction. **USA showing signs of emerging from the recession** Just as North America was at the forefront of the plunge into recession, it is also showing signs of being amongst the first to emerge from recession. The maximum impact of the Obama administration’s stimulus package has been felt this summer and the pick-up in US manufacturing capacity and the positive impact that this has had on its northern neighbour, Canada, should see economic momentum build during the coming months. As of August US industrial production has posted two consecutive months of month-on-month growth, the first time that this has occurred since November and December of 2007. However, 7M jobs have been lost since the beginning of the recession and, according to the US labour department, in August, 26.3M workers were underutilised, of which 14.9M were unemployed. The unemployment rate of 9.7% was its highest since 1983. This pool Metals Market Service Monthly Update – September 2009 P

of unemployed and underemployed workers will act as a drag on consumer spending and the housing markets and, as a consequence, the US recovery will likely be tempered for much of next year and it will not be until 2011 that growth gets fully underway. 

**IP data highlight the extent of the downturn in US manufacturing** An indication of the extent of the collapse in US manufacturing comes from the latest estimates of industrial production and capacity utilisation published by the Federal Reserve.  These show that utilisation rates in the manufacturing sector in August were just 66.6%, well below the 19722008 average rate of 79.6% and lower than that seen in the recessions of the 1970s and early 1980s.  Based on the response following previous US recessions, and even when helped by the permanent elimination of unwanted/obsolete capacity, utilisation rates are likely to take 2-5 years to recover to pre-recession levels. 

**US housing market stabilising** The recession began with the housing market which, after falling since 2006, seems to be stabilising, with the number of housing starts creeping towards the upper end of the 500-600k unit range seen this year.  Although this rate is extremely low, it is allowing for the draw down of excessive inventories of new homes built during the bubble.  However, demand for new homes is likely to be hit around the end of the year as the number of foreclosures builds.  It is unlikely that there will be a dramatic acceleration in the pace of construction of new homes until inventories are drawn down, a process which will probably take two to three years to complete, which suggests that demand growth for copper from this sector will be restrained at best.  Whereas the residential construction sector is showing some signs of stability, the non-residential construction sector will decline well into next year.  The US National Association of Realtors is forecasting that annual rents for office, industrial and retail properties are forecast to decline by 6-14% this year and by 5-12% next year.  Declining rents and increasing vacancy rates are likely to slow the construction of new properties for much of 2010.  Further evidence of the likely weakness in the US non-residential construction sector comes from the American Institute of Architects’ billing index which reached 43.1 in July.  While this was five points higher than in June, it was well below the 50 level which separates expanding demand for its members services from contraction.  The weakness of the index suggests that non-residential construction sector will remain depressed well into 2010.  This weakness will undermine any strength in demand for copper wire and cable and copper plumbing and air conditioning tube. 

**Automotive sector still a drag on the US economy** The other drag on the US economy will continue to be the automotive sector, which despite the boost from the cash for clunkers programme will emerge from

the recession a shadow of its former self. While the ‘cash for clunkers’ programme lifted US car sales by 16% in year on year terms in August and total light vehicle sales by 1%, it has not been enough to make a major difference to the year to date figures which remain appalling. Total light vehicle sales in the first eight months of the year fell annually by 28% to 7M units. The situation is even worse in terms of production, with output of cars and light trucks through to August totalling just 3.3M units, down 47% year on year. According to local press reports the union is seeking a 5.5% pay increase while management has apparently offered a rise of around 1%.  In Peru, an agreement between management and unions still appears to be a long way off although production continues without an immediate thereat of strike action.  It seems that the unions want to negotiate every two years while the company would prefer a sixyear cycle.  Elsewhere, in Zambia a one day strike at the 16kt/a Chibuluma South mine resulted in a minimal loss of production.  Workers are seeking a 30% wage hike, which is 25% higher than management’s current offer.

**Chinese firms to fast track Aynak mine project development** Newly-formed company, Metallurgical Corp. of China and its partner, Jiangxi Copper expect to fast track their Aynak copper project in Afghanistan with the objective of commencing production in 2011.  Construction work has reportedly already commenced at site and the phase I development programme will result in an annual production of 180kt of copper in concentrates, rising to 320kt/a in phase II.  This schedule is especially aggressive given the general lack of infrastructure in the vicinity.  There is a requirement, for example, to build a 400MW power plant and railway facilities.  The Chinese consortium was awarded the project by the Afghan government after bidding $808M in November 2007.  Previous exploration during the 1970s by Soviet geologists identified a resource of 700Mt of ore grading 1.26% Cu. 

**Jiangxi Copper to raise refinery capacity to 1Mt/a by 2012** Jiangxi Copper plans to raise its refined copper capacity to 1Mt/a by 2012.  This is equivalent to a 10% uplift on its current level.  At the same time the company aims to increase domestic mine production from 169kt/a currently, to 210kt/a over the next few years.  Separately, Jiangxi Copper will have the right to receive 50% of the production from its part-owned Aynak project (see above). 

**PPC is keen to develop its Caserones project** PPC recently announced plans to progress its Caserones project in Chile.  PPC, which gained the right to the project in May 2006 estimates that an initial investment of $1.86Bn will be needed for the project.  Caserones will have a thirty-year mine life, producing 90-150kt/a of copper-in-concentrates and a further 30kt/a of SxEw Cu as well as 3kt/a of Mo.  All concentrates would be smelted at the company’s two facilities (Saganoseki and Tamano) in Japan thereby raising PPC’s concentrate feed self sufficiency from the current 18% to ~40%.  Current plans are to commence construction during H2 2010 and bring the mine on stream in January 2013, subject to permitting. 

**Russian H1 2009 refined production declines by 10% year on year** Russia’s refined

copper output fell by ~10% year on year during the first half of 2009, from 439kt to 395kt. The largest decline was seen within the UGMK group which was almost entirely the result of lower scrap availability. The company’s sole refinery at Pyshma recorded a reduction of 29kt (i.e. 149kt in comparison with last year’s H1 output of 178kt). Elsewhere, Norilsk’s Polar and Kola divisions produced less refined copper (185kt vs 197kt), due to lower copper ore grades. Ironically, Russian cathode exports more than doubled in H1 2009, year on year (190kt vs 85kt) but this was purely on account of the removal of the 5% export duty on cathodes (previously there had been an incentive to convert cathode into wire rod which is exempt from export duties).
